If I follow things down it seems that it just builds a MainChain and will fail if this is not the case. Looking at the example code, I guess I assumed that the absence of side chains in those places was just because it was an example, not that it was required as such. Is this something likely to change in the future? If not why would we want to user to pass these - would it make sense to define the side chain sequences as things that can be set - i.e length main chain - 3 so the first side chain in the sequence applies to main bead 3 (assuming indexes start at 1). Maybe passing them is clearer in that then each main has a side chain entry. But I think the behavior of 1st/2nd and last needs to be surfaced.
PS. Now that I know this I notice all the test cases are like that with 1st/2nd and last side chains empty, which I guess I expect now but had not really noticed before.

Oh the error text here still talks about Non-None which presumably should be updated.

body:
There are multiple aspects here:

1. 1st, 2nd and last not allowed: this is clearly documented in the Peptide's docstrings. The docstrings states that "this can be done without loss of generality" and refers to the paper for more information.

2. changing the side chain sequence: I don't think, that this is a good idea. Simply in terms of usability, I find it difficult to justify why a list `["a", "b", "c"]` would attach to some main sequence `"ABCDEF"` at the positions `a -> C`, `b -> D` and `c -> E`. That is both, not easy to document or explain and also just confusing. I would then rather see a good warning for the user.

3. Unittests: I am not sure if this exists already, but arguably there should be some unittests which assert the correct warnings being raised in edge cases similar to this.
